newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire spotlight on Mobutu, talks next week?.
newsitem.headline: Zaire spotlight on Mobutu, talks next week?.

text.p: Rebels are ratcheting up the pressure on Zaire's ailing and embattled President Mobutu Sese Seko as calls for the veteran strongman to quit proliferate.

With many of Mobutu's one-time allies urging him to stand aside, South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told reporters in Washington on Thursday that there was no suggestion as yet that the Zairean president would want to seek asylum.
"I don't think we would respond negatively," he added after talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright when asked about South Africa's response to any request.

The rebels, who control half the sprawling Central African nation including its economic heartland, have paused in their relentless advance and have given him until the weekend to signal that he is ready to quit.

Mbeki, who hosted a first round of talks between the warring parties last week, said he hoped negotiations would resume early next week and that he expected the question of Mobutu's future to be on the agenda.

"What happens to the governance of Zaire is something that is on the agenda of the negotiations...and I'm sure that will be included, the future of Mobutu," he added. "It's not a matter that can be decided outside of that process of negotiation."
The governor of the mining province of Shaba, waiting for word from rebel leader Laurent Kabila on his future in the job, said on Friday it was time for the ailing president to go.

"Mobutu must retire now because of his health rather than continuing a war that is futile," Kyungu wa Kumwanza told reporters in Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city and capital of Shaba. Mobutu had prostate cancer surgery in Europe in August.

The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis. They ended the battle for Lubumbashi on Thursday, driving Mobutu loyalists from its airport and into the bush.
In Kinshasa, Mobutu, who has held sway over Africa's third largest country since a 1965 coup, had talks on Thursday with his new emergency rule prime minister General Likulia Bolongo.
The capital, rocked by clashes between Mobutu's army and supporters of ousted prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi on Wednesday, waited for Likulia to announce his government.
Radical opposition leader Tshisekedi, shunted aside after under a week in the job, has accused Mobutu of treason and urged Zaireans to step up pressure to force him from power.
Former colonial power Belgium says Mobutu engineered a military coup to cling on to power and denounces what it calls "a military dictatorship" in Kinshasa.

The United States, which helped prop up Mobutu during the Cold War fearing the spread of communism in strategic parts of Africa, says it was time for the veteran strongman to go. The State Department has urged an end to "dictatorship" in Zaire.
But France, a long-time Mobutu ally, called for an orderly transition and questioned Kabila's democratic credentials -- casting doubts on whether he would call elections.

Kabila gave Mobutu three days from Thursday to signal his willingness to stand down. "I am waiting for a little period of three days for Mobutu to make a decision to contact us to negotiate his departure," he said at Mobutu's former palace in the eastern town Goma, now used as rebel headquarters.
"If this doesn't happen we will be forced to advance on all fronts," Kabila said.
